Row.Text: Citizens emigrate from unhappy, struggling cities to happier, more prosperous ones, both within and between civilizations, driven by a Prosperity model (food, production, happiness, war, siege, starvation). Migration counts are reported as historically representative populations, aligned with the Demographics mod's scaling.
How emigration reports the number of people who move. "Both" shows the Civ population number and the historically-scaled people count (matching the Demographics mod); the others show only one.
Open the full set of Emigration tuning knobs in a separate window. These are starting points, not playtested-balanced values; the intensity preset above sets sensible defaults for most of them.

Pin the wars and disasters that drove migration onto the migration network's playback timeline, so a spike can be traced back to what caused it. Hover a pin to name the event; click it to scrub there. Display only — it never changes who moves. Only events recorded from now on can be pinned: wars and disasters from earlier in an existing save were never stamped with the turn they happened.

Add a "Diversity" tab to the migration dashboard ranking your settlements by how mixed their people's origins are — the civilizations they originally came from — with a colour-coded bar per settlement showing that mix against its population. Display only: it reads the population origins the mod already tracks, changes nothing about who moves, and grants no yields.

Add a "Character" column to the diversity ranking summarising each settlement as Homogeneous, Local Majority, Mixed City, Cosmopolitan Center or World City, blended from its origin mix, its border openness and how many people are arriving. Purely descriptive: it grants no yields and does not affect migration.

How many settlements the "Most diverse settlements" ranking lists at the top of the tab. The full "All settlements" list below it always shows every settlement, whatever this is set to. Only used when the ranking is on.

Show a "why?" breakdown in the settlement readout and the Prosperity lens tooltip: which pressures are driving people out, and what is drawing them to where they are going, each as a share of the total. Display only: it reports the reasoning the mod already uses to move people, changes nothing about who moves, and grants no yields.
Each settlement's people, coloured by the civilization they originally came from. Bar width shows population.
Every settlement you can see, by civilization.
Describes where each settlement's people came from — not its Cultural Enclaves. No yields attached.

Overall migration intensity, sets how often people move AND how hard wars uproot them: the per-turn limits, the war-refugee burst size, and the per-city loss cap. Low = gentle; High = heavy. Changes take effect within a turn. "Custom" leaves your Advanced values as-is. For finer control, adjust the individual knobs in Advanced settings below.
Pressure a settlement must build before one population point emigrates. Lower = more frequent emigration.
Turns a settlement rests before it can lose another population point.
Cap on how many population points move across the whole world each pass.
Pacing: max migrants per city per turn

The most population points one settlement can lose to migration in a single turn — the direct cap that stops a city emptying out during a siege. Deaths are a separate channel, not counted here. The intensity preset sets this (Low 1 / Medium 2 / High 4).
Pacing: max arrivals per city per turn

The most population points one settlement can gain from migration in a single turn — the symmetric cap that stops a single boomtown absorbing dozens of migrants at once. The intensity preset sets this (Low 2 / Medium 4 / High 8).
Run the emigration pass once every N of your turns. Raise it to ease per-turn cost on large saves, and, if the Demographics mod is installed, lower its sample frequency first.
If off, people only move between cities of the same civilization.
Whether minor / city-state settlements take part in migration.
Only consider foreign cities your civilization has met.

Apply small, hand-tuned per-leader and per-civilization adjustments (magnet damping, integration speed, war-time retention, source bias) so outliers behave distinctly. Off = every civilization uses the same global model.

How far the per-leader/civ adjustments are allowed to diverge from the global model. 1.0 = full distinct identities; lower values flatten the differences between civilizations toward the same model to curb snowballing; 0 = fully flat (same as turning the table off).
Enable the Pro- / Anti-Immigration Stance cards' effect on immigration (the cards are added in the policy menu and cost or grant Influence). Off = the stances have no migration effect.

How much immigration the Anti-Immigration Stance lets through (0.4 = about 60% turned away, and any refugees you do admit settle more slowly). Lower = more closed. Only used when border policies are on.

How strongly the Anti-Immigration Stance keeps your own people from leaving for rival civilizations (0.6 = their pull toward other civilizations cut to 60%; 1 = off). Lower = stronger retention. Only used when border policies are on.
How much the Pro-Immigration Stance increases immigration (1.5 = +50%). Higher = more open. Only used when border policies are on.
How much per-capita food pulls migrants toward a city.
How much per-capita production (the "work available" proxy) pulls migrants.
How strongly a city's net happiness attracts migrants.
How much a city's size counts against it (so small thriving towns still attract).

Replace the flat happiness weight with a nuanced model: happiness is measured against the world average, a happy city's pull levels off (no runaway magnet) while misery still strongly repels, and happiness amplifies a city's economy instead of dwarfing it. Off = the simpler flat happiness weight.
How many points above the world-average happiness count as "very happy" before the pull saturates. Higher = happiness keeps mattering longer. Only used by the shaped model.
How much a happy city's economy is amplified (and a miserable one suppressed) as a migration draw. Only used by the shaped model.
Credit back some of the unhappiness a city suffers purely from urban overcrowding, so a deliberately tall/dense city isn't double-punished (its density already suppresses its yields). 0 = off.
Urban population a city can hold before overcrowding counts against it (mirrors the game's overcrowding threshold). Only used when the discount is on.
Score penalty per point of accumulated combat intensity in a city's borders.
Ceiling on the violence penalty, so a rout saturates rather than runs away.
How fast accumulated violence fades with no new fighting (lower = fades faster).
War: violence needed to flee an invader
Minimum violence before refugees flee directionally away from the nearest enemy.
War: weight of fresh city damage
Intensity added when a city takes new district damage in a turn (an assault spike).
Intensity added each turn while a city center stays damaged.
War: weight per pillaged tile (0 = off)
Intensity per pillaged improvement in a city's borders, per turn. 0 skips the scan.
War: use the siege model (capped + escalating)

Make war-driven emigration escalate the longer a city is besieged, but cap the total a city can lose to war so it can't be fully depopulated without a capture (the remnant digs in). Off = the simpler flat violence penalty.
How many turns a siege must last to reach its full emigration pressure (a fresh raid starts gentle and ramps up). Only used by the siege model.
War (siege): max share lost to war
The most of a city's population (as a fraction of its size when the siege began) that war-driven emigration can take before it stops. Only used by the siege model.
War: refugee surge per turn (1 = off)

The most rural population a heavily besieged city can shed in a single turn. War refugees then leave in bursts that scale with the intensity of the fighting, instead of a steady one-per-turn trickle, still bounded by the siege loss cap. 1 = off (the old trickle).

How strongly refugees fleeing a war avoid the civilization that attacked them, preferring their own cities first, then any third party, and the aggressor last. 0 = off (refugees ignore who started the war).
How strongly war refugees prefer to resettle within their own civilization before crossing to another. Only used when "avoid the aggressor" is on.
Pull penalty per hex between source and destination. Higher = more local migration.
How strongly refugees prefer destinations away from the nearest invader.
Extra reluctance to migrate across a civilization border.

How strongly a civilization in acute crisis (war/disaster) pushes its refugees to flee ACROSS BORDERS to another empire, rather than relocating to its own (equally-stricken) cities and dying there. Higher = more cross-civ escape. 0 = off.
How much a base-game Open Borders agreement between two civilizations eases migration between them, both directions. 0 = off.

The longest a migrant can spend traveling before arriving. They leave the source the turn they depart; the actual delay scales with the distance to their destination (farther = longer), up to this cap. War refugees always take at least a turn. If their destination is destroyed while they are en route, they perish in transit. 0 = instant arrival.

Integration "load" added to the receiving civilization for each migrant it absorbs. The civilization pays a per-turn cost proportional to its current load, which decays over the integration duration. 0 = off.
Multiplies the load added by (1 + this × destination population), so absorbing into a large settlement adds more — a brake on runaway population magnets.
How fast the integration load fades each turn — this sets the duration of the cost. Lower = shorter (migrants integrate faster); higher = the cost lingers longer.
Integration: happiness per turn per load
Happiness drained each turn per unit of integration load. 0 = off. (If it has no effect in your game, use the gold cost instead.)
Integration: gold per turn per load
Gold drained each turn per unit of integration load, including across civilizations. 0 = off.
Cost: happiness per held migrant unit

Happiness drained each turn per held migrant a civilization has not yet settled, scaling with the count, so overflow migrants must be settled, not hoarded. 0 = off. (If it has no effect in your game, use the gold cost instead.)
Cost: gold per held migrant unit
Gold drained each turn per held migrant a civilization is holding, scaling with the count. 0 = off.

Make a civilization that's absorbing lots of migrants a less attractive destination for further migration (it's busy integrating newcomers), scaling with how much it's digesting. A structural brake on runaway magnets. 0 = off.

Make a civilization whose population has run far ahead of the field a less attractive destination for cross-civ migration — a self-correcting brake on a runaway leader that grows with its lead (0 off / 8 gentle / 15 standard / 28 strong). It never impedes the leader's OUTflow or internal moves. 0 = off.

How far a civilization's population may run ahead of the world-average civilization before the anti-snowball headwind starts to bite, as a multiple of fair share. Lower = the brake engages sooner (more egalitarian); higher = only an extreme runaway leader is slowed.

When a foreign diaspora grows into an established community in one of your cities, offer a one-time choice (embrace, tax, or let be) with a small yield reward and drawback, and track a persistent per-city enclave that turns "contested" (its yield benefit is reduced and it adds a small happiness strain) while you are at war with its homeland. Off = no enclave decisions or contested strain.
How much of a city a single foreign origin must make up before it can become a Cultural Enclave. Higher = rarer enclaves, as fewer cities ever qualify.

The smallest standing population (in city-size points) a single foreign origin must reach before it can form a Cultural Enclave, so a tiny community can't qualify on share alone. Lower = small settlements can host enclaves too.

How strongly a foreign community that has reached a foothold resists blending into the host, so it can grow into a full enclave instead of being absorbed first. Stronger = enclaves form more readily; Off = communities integrate at the normal rate and rarely reach the enclave threshold.

How many turns an established community must persist before its one-time enclave decision is offered, so a brief spike (such as a war-refugee wave that later moves on) never triggers a permanent enclave. A short dip below the threshold is forgiven. 0 = offer as soon as the community forms.
Minimum turns between two Cultural Enclave decisions. Higher = the offers are spaced further apart.
The most Cultural Enclave decisions that can be offered in a single age. Lower = fewer enclave choices each age.

Testing aid. While on, your largest qualifying foreign community is offered its Cultural Enclave decision right away, skipping the persistence wait, the per-age limit, and the wait behind other events, and accepting a community that has only reached a foothold. It still needs the minimum population. Turn off once you've seen the decision.
Let environmental disasters (floods, volcanoes, plagues, …) push population out of struck cities as climate/disaster refugees, alongside war and unhappiness. Off = disasters don't affect migration.
How strongly accumulated disaster distress in a city pushes its people to leave. Only used when disasters drive migration.
How fast a disaster's distress fades once it passes (lower = fades faster). Only used when disasters drive migration.
Disasters: scale damage by measured impact

A disaster's population hit tracks what it actually did to the city (tiles pillaged, yields cut, buildings damaged), bounded by its type. A storm that pillages nothing is nearly free; a catastrophic volcano still hurts. Off restores the old flat per-type damage.
How much a minor disaster still stings (lower lifts small impacts more; 1.0 is straight-line). Only used when damage scales by measured impact.
Disasters: even out cost across game speeds

On slow speeds a disaster's distress lingers for more turns; this softens the per-turn bite so the TOTAL cost is about the same on Marathon as on Standard. Off pays the full per-turn hit every one of those extra turns (the old, harsher behaviour).
Let refugees fleeing an infected city seed a smaller outbreak-distress at their destination, migration as a contagion vector, beyond the game's trade-network spread.
How chatty migration notifications are: 0 = off, 1 = important only (refugee crises and severe disasters, the default), 2 = verbose (a summary every turn there's notable migration).
Only notify for disasters at or above this severity (0 = even minor events, 3 = only legendary ones like a great eruption). Minor disasters still affect migration silently.

Which disasters pop up on screen (the log always keeps every severe one): 0 = off, log only; 1 = only disasters that strike a settlement, so they drive migration (the default); 2 = any disaster at or above the minimum severity. Pair with "min disaster severity" to set the bar.
The fewest turns between important notifications, so they can't bunch up. 0 = no limit.
Show "world news" alerts when another civilization hits a major refugee crisis. Off = only notifications about your own settlements. On by default.
How many people (cumulative) a civilization must displace before a refugee-crisis headline fires, once per multiple crossed, so a long war makes a few headlines, not one per turn.
Show an on-demand panel explaining why a selected settlement is gaining or losing population: the dominant cause, where its people are pulled, the integration cost, and what you can do about it.

Add a small bar strip to the per-city readout showing its net migration over the last several passes (green bars for gaining, red for losing), so you can tell at a glance whether things are getting better or worse.

Show a floating "Self-Test" button in-game that runs live diagnostics for the reported issues (settlement coverage, cultural enclaves, the two population measures, notifications, persistence) and can force the enclave pop-up and a test toast on demand — no developer console needed. For troubleshooting; leave off for normal play. Takes effect after reloading the save.
Outlet: attrition when there's no refuge

Keep migration from being a closed system: a trapped, badly distressed city (siege, starvation, heavy violence or disaster) with nowhere viable to flee loses population — people die or scatter rather than stay forever.

How dire a city's situation (siege/starvation/violence/disaster, as a percentage penalty) must be before trapped population starts to die off. Higher = only the most desperate cities. Only used when the outlet is on.
Pressure a trapped, distressed city must build before it loses one population point. Lower = faster die-off. Only used when the outlet is on.

Emigration adds living population movement to the world. Each turn, citizens leave unhappy, struggling, or war-torn settlements and resettle in happier, more prosperous ones, within your civilization and across borders to others.[n][n]Where people go is decided by a Prosperity model that weighs each city's happiness, yields, and situation, shaped by distance so migration stays regional. Receiving migrants is not free: a civilization pays an integration cost as newcomers settle in.[n][n]The world also keeps a memory of who moved. Every settlement tracks the civilizations its people descend from, shown on the map by the Ethnic Composition lens. Newcomers slowly take on their host's identity, diasporas return home once their homeland recovers, and the great waves are written up as history in the Migration Chronicle.[n][n]Most of the system's deeper behaviours (refugees that shun an aggressor, border policies, disasters, ethnic integration, return migration, and the occasional refugee decision) are on by default and can be switched off in Options, under Mods, Emigration.

What does and does not drive migration (most of it tunable in Options, under Mods, Emigration). A full version is on the dashboard's Guide tab.[n][n]✓ Your civilization and other major civilizations move population, whether or not you have met them.[n]✗ City-states, minor civilizations, and Independent Powers do not send or receive population.[n]✓ Unhappiness, low yields, war damage, sieges (including attacks by a city-state or Independent Power), pillaging, starvation, plague, disasters, and overcrowding all push people out.[n]✓ Prosperity, high happiness, a Pro-Immigration Stance, Open Borders, and a nearby location attract them.[n]✗ Migrants are not instant (distance adds delay) and not free (a temporary integration cost); war alone cannot empty a city without capturing it.[n]✓ A settlement gains or loses only so many people per turn (a per-city cap each way, scaled by the intensity preset) so neither a siege empties a city in one turn nor a boomtown swallows dozens at once; arrivals over the cap wait in transit, and refugees with nowhere to land perish on the road.[n][n]Emigration does not change AI decisions or replace base-game files. Unmet civilizations are simulated but hidden until you reveal them.

Every settlement is scored for Prosperity from its per-capita yields and, above all, its net happiness. An unhappy city steadily loses people to happier, wealthier ones even in peacetime, while a small penalty for sheer size keeps thriving towns from becoming bottomless magnets.[n][n]People prefer nearby destinations, so migration spreads outward across the region rather than leaping across the map. War, siege, starvation, unrest, and disaster all sharply lower a city's Prosperity, turning it into a source of refugees.

A city only sheds war refugees when there is actual violence inside its borders, damage to its districts, or pillaging on its land, not merely because its empire is at war. The longer a siege grinds on, the more it drives people out, but a city can never be fully emptied by war alone: short of an outright capture, a remnant always digs in.[n][n]Refugees flee away from the nearest invader. With aggressor avoidance enabled, they also prefer their own civilization first, then any neutral power, and treat the civilization that attacked them as a destination of last resort.[n][n]Resettlement is neither instant nor guaranteed. Migrants spend a few turns in transit, and a city can only take in so many newcomers in a single turn (just as a stricken city can only shed so many) so arrivals beyond that cap wait and try again, the longest-waiting first. If the haven they were fleeing toward is captured or razed while they travel, or it stays too full to receive them, those refugees perish in transit, counted among the losses rather than as new arrivals.[n][n]People who flee are not gone forever. Once their original homeland is at peace with their host and prospering again, a fraction of those living abroad set out for home over time, a slow return rather than a snap-back. And when a great wave reaches your own lands, driven by a neighbour's conquests or a plague, you are occasionally asked how to receive them: take them in, settle them on the frontier, or turn them away. These refugee decisions are rare by design and can be switched off in Options.

Absorbing migrants is not free. Each newcomer adds an integration load to the receiving civilization, which pays a per-turn cost (in gold and in happiness) until that load fades over the integration period. A civilization that keeps pulling people in keeps paying.[n][n]A congestion effect can further make a civilization that is busy settling new arrivals a less attractive destination for still more, a brake that wealth alone does not remove. Together these keep any single civilization from snowballing into a dominant migration magnet for the world's people.[n][n]Integration also has a slower, cultural side, separate from the gold and happiness cost above. Over many turns, newcomers take on their host civilization's identity within each settlement's ethnic makeup, so a peaceful, settled city gradually absorbs a diaspora. War with a diaspora's homeland, or unrest in the city, holds that integration back, leaving a distinct community that keeps its colour on the Ethnic Composition lens.

Two levers shape migration across your borders. Your own stance is a policy card, available in every age. Slot the Pro-Immigration Stance to welcome the world: more migrants arrive, and your cosmopolitan reputation earns a little Influence each turn. Or slot the Anti-Immigration Stance to close yourself off: fewer newcomers arrive and fewer of your own people leave for rivals, and a mobilized home economy adds Production in every city, though the world judges your isolation with a steady Influence drain. Choose whichever fits your strategy.[n][n]Diplomacy matters too. When you and another civilization sign an Open Borders agreement, migrants flow more freely between your two lands, in both directions.

Where the stance policies decide whether your borders are open, a second set of cards decides what you make of the people who pass through them. The Talent Attraction, Cultural Magnetism, and Commercial Draw policies turn immigration into an engine: every newcomer you draw banks a growing dividend of Science, Culture, or Gold that compounds while people keep arriving and fades once the inflow stops, a counterpart to the integration cost, rewarding civilizations that sustain attraction.[n][n]The Asylum policies answer a different call. Throwing your doors open to those fleeing war and catastrophe draws refugees toward you, the most desperate first, and the world remembers the gesture in Influence, with the later compact enriching your Culture besides. Together they let a welcoming people benefit from openness rather than merely endure it.

Attraction need not wait for migration to come to you. From the diplomacy screen you can aim a Talent Raid, Cultural Offensive, or Commercial Offensive at a rival, a sustained campaign to bend their people toward your cities. For as long as it runs you pay Influence each turn, and in return that rival's migration tilts your way, drawing off their brightest minds, cultural figures, or merchants; each one who arrives banks the matching Science, Culture, or Gold dividend, the same as a willing immigrant.[n][n]It is a strategic competition tool, not war: no city is attacked and no border is crossed by force, yet a stronger neighbour's talent can be quietly drained to your benefit for the price of sustained diplomatic effort.

Environmental disasters (floods, volcanoes, plagues, and more) drive people out of stricken cities as climate and disaster refugees, alongside war and unhappiness. The worse the event, the harder it pushes; minor events only nudge migration quietly.[n][n]Plague is doubly dangerous: an infected city both loses population and, if migrants carry the contagion, can seed a smaller outbreak wherever its refugees settle, spreading disease along the very roads of flight.

Migration is not a sealed system. When a city is desperate, under siege, starving, or devastated by disaster, and there is nowhere safe left to flee, its trapped population does not simply wait forever. People die or scatter, and the city loses population with no destination.[n][n]Even when there is still somewhere to run, a lethal crisis claims some who cannot escape in time. These losses start small and grow the longer the crisis drags on, then ease again once it lifts, so a sudden blow is survivable while a grinding siege or famine is not. They are not capped: a long enough catastrophe can wear a city's rural population all the way down, though its urban districts and the settlement itself hold until an actual capture.[n][n]This outlet is a measure of last resort. A content city that merely has nowhere better to go is left alone, and the loss is counted as deaths, kept separate from the refugees who reach a new home.

A handful of leaders and civilizations feel migration differently, so their historical character shows through. These are small, bounded adjustments on top of the global rules, not large enough to trigger runaway growth, and they apply only while per-civilization tuning is on (it is, by default).[n][n]Leaders whose happiness would otherwise make cities dominant migration magnets pull a little less strongly: Benjamin Franklin most of all, with Isabella, Ashoka, and Rizal also reined in. Wealthy conquerors find spoils costlier to settle — Isabella and Xerxes pay more to absorb the people they win.[n][n]Tall, specialist-minded powers are shielded from overcrowding so their dense cities aren't punished twice: Pachacuti, and the Abbasids most of all. Fast-growing peoples whose numbers outrun their prosperity get a small cushion to keep their citizens, Confucius, the Han, and the Qing, while the Khmer are spared the worst of their own non-capital unhappiness. And realms built behind strong walls, the Normans and the English, hold their population through a siege far better than the unwalled.

Emigration simulates the whole world from the first turn: every living major civilization, not only the ones you have met. This keeps migration honest: people flow according to the real state of the world, and a city you later conquer carries the true origin history of its people.[n][n]To avoid spoilers, the dashboard, the graphs, and the map lens only SHOW civilizations you have met. Unmet civilizations are still calculated in the background, but hidden from view by default, so you don't learn about rivals you haven't encountered yet. You can widen what is shown through the shared analytics-visibility setting (the same one the Demographics mod uses): your own civilization only, met civilizations, or all.[n][n]In short: everything is simulated, and what you see is up to you. Simulation scope (whole world or met-only) and on-screen visibility are independent settings.

Open the Migration dashboard from its button on the in-game dock, or from the Migration page in the Demographics mod. It is organised into tabs:[n][n]• A migration network, an animated view of civilizations sized by how much population moves through them, with dots flowing along the routes.[n]• A flow map, the same flows drawn as arrows you can follow down to individual cities.[n]• A civilizations ledger of arrivals, departures, net change, refugees, and losses.[n]• A breakdown of why people move, by cause.[n]• A settlements list, ranked by how close each is to losing people.[n]• A policies view, showing who has adopted a Pro- or Anti-Immigration Stance.[n]• A Migration Chronicle, a written history of the world's great migrations: cities emptied by war or disaster, diasporas taking root far from home, and peoples returning once their homeland recovered.[n]• A Guide with a quick reference of what does and does not drive migration.[n][n]On the map itself, the Ethnic Composition lens (Shift+E) paints each settlement as a per-tile mosaic by the origin of its people, the dense urban core in the dominant origin's colour and smaller communities spread across its tiles, and hovering a settled tile adds the exact mix to its tooltip.

Every settlement records where its people came from, by the civilization each person descends from, and keeps that record through conquest. The Ethnic Composition lens (Shift+E) shows it as a per-tile mosaic: the dense urban core in the dominant origin's colour, smaller communities spread across its tiles, with the exact mix in each settled tile's tooltip.[n][n]Over time, newcomers integrate into their host civilization, unless war with their homeland or unrest in the city keeps a community distinct. And once a homeland is at peace with its host and prospering again, return migration draws a fraction of its people back home over time, moving real population. All of this is on by default and can be switched off in Options.

When a foreign community grows into a lasting part of one of your cities — a real presence living there now, not just a memory of past arrivals — it takes root as a Cultural Enclave, a district at the city's edge named for the origin people. You are offered a one-time choice of how the city makes room for it: two options drawn from that civilization's own character, each a small benefit paired with a matching drawback, or simply let them be. The stance you choose is applied to your empire's yields each turn.[n][n]Each enclave reads as a page of history, carrying one short, real historical quote in the origin people's own language beside its English translation. A single origin civilization can hold at most two enclaves across your empire; the cap is counted per origin, so a Roman and a Norman enclave never crowd each other out. Enclaves persist, can change hands as a city's population shifts, and grow restless if you go to war with their homeland.

The Migration Chronicle, on its own tab in the dashboard, writes the world's great migrations as short history: a city emptied by war or disaster, a diaspora taking root far from home, a people returning once their homeland recovered. The per-event detail still lives in the Notifications log; the Chronicle is the story.[n][n]Once in a while, when a real upheaval (a neighbour conquering several cities in a short span, or a plague crisis) sends a wave of refugees toward your lands, you are asked how to receive them: welcome them in, settle them on the frontier, or turn them away. These decisions are rare and lightly weighted, and can be switched off in Options. A civilization you have not met is named only as hearsay, never revealed.

The main peacetime driver. Happiness is still the single biggest factor, but after the 1.4.1 rebalance a city's per-capita yields carry a real share of the decision too, so both an unhappy city AND a low-yield one bleed people, and a city that's both empties fastest. Unhappy settlements are doubly hit: 1.4.1 also suppresses their yields, which the prosperity score reads directly.

Damage to ANY of the city's districts (its center or an outer urban/rural quarter) is read from game state (fog-independent) and scales the war penalty. An assault that wrecks only the city's edge still registers, even while the center reads pristine.

Attacked by a city-state / Independent Power
Same per-city conflict pressure as a major-civ war: an Independent/minor raid on a city still drives THAT city's people out, attacker-agnostic.
Pillaged tiles in the city's borders
Pillaged improvements on the city's own plots count as violence in its borders (polled, fog-independent); more pillaged tiles means more pressure.

A city with negative NET food is flagged starving: most of its people flee to better-fed cities, and, because famine kills those who can't escape in time, some also DIE (a death, not a migration). It clears once net food recovers.

Environmental-disaster distress adds a per-city penalty on a capped sliding scale, scaled by the disaster's real impact (its yield/damage tables, not the weak Severity flag). Like any lethal crisis it both displaces people AND kills some who can't flee. An eruption/flood strikes every city around its epicenter, so a volcano on unowned border terrain still hits the neighbouring cities' people.
Urban population above a threshold adds pressure (the overcrowding term); the per-leader tuning can soften it via the overcrowding discount.

No. Three brakes compound: the field-relative prosperity model (every city is judged against the world average, so no single magnet's pull runs away without limit), a congestion headwind on a civilization digesting a fresh surge of arrivals, and a self-correcting anti-snowball brake: the further a civilization's population runs ahead of the world average, the stronger the headwind against further migration INTO it (it never slows a leader's own people leaving, only newcomers piling in). The 1.4.1 rebalance was snowball-checked and, by judging cities against a less-crushed field, actually narrows the gap that feeds a leader rather than widening it. Where do people go when they leave?
To the nearest higher-prosperity settlement they can reach. Migration is distance-penalized, so people move regionally, not to the single best city on the map.
Away from the nearest enemy, preferring their own civilization first, then neutral civilizations, and the attacker last.
How many people move, and how often?

War- and disaster-driven refugees flee every turn; voluntary (prosperity/unhappiness) migration is more gradual, resting briefly between moves. Each civilization migrates on its own per-turn budget that scales with its size and active crises, so simultaneous wars never throttle one another. Counts show as scaled people or raw population points (your choice), and the whole sim runs on a turn interval you can lengthen in Options for large saves.
Do people die, or just move away?

Both, depending on the cause. Ordinary (prosperity / unhappiness) migration NEVER kills; people simply leave for better cities. But a LETHAL crisis (war, siege, disaster, or famine) also kills some who can't escape in time: those deaths leave the world entirely (shown in the Losses/deaths tally, separate from refugees), even while the rest flee. So a city under crisis loses people two ways at once: most flee, a few die. The death toll builds up gradually rather than striking all at once, growing the longer the crisis drags on and easing if it lifts, so a brief scare is recoverable while a grinding siege or famine is not. Separately, a refugee can also perish IN TRANSIT if the city they were fleeing to is captured or razed before they arrive, or stays too full to take them in.
What happens when I capture or lose a city?

Its existing residents stay coded to the civilization they came FROM (the prior owner), not to you. The Ethnic Composition lens paints the city's tiles in that origin's colour (a per-tile mosaic), and on the network diagram their dots keep the old civilization's colour and name; only NEW population born after the capture counts as yours. So a conquered city carries real origin history that fades only as it regrows and its newcomers integrate. War can shrink it, but only an actual capture transfers it.
My city shrank from size 12 to 5 in a war, will it grow back?

Yes. War displacement only moves population points; it never razes districts or deletes buildings (only the base game's own conquest does that). You keep the larger city's infrastructure with fewer people, and it regrows two ways, both additive: the base game's normal food growth (untouched), and immigration: once the fighting stops and its prosperity recovers, the surviving high-yield buildings/districts make it an attractive destination, so migrants move in and population is added back.
Do the same refugees who fled come back?

Some now do, once the homeland recovers. Most resettle permanently where they fled, but Return Migration adds a homeward pull: when a diaspora's original civilization is at peace with their host and faring well again, a fraction set out for home over time, moving real population back. It's a slow ebb over many turns, never a snap-back, and it only flows while relations stay peaceful. A war-torn city still regrows mainly from births and new immigrants; returns are an additional, gentler source once peace and prosperity return. You can switch return migration off in Options.
Does repairing pillaged tiles restore the lost population?

No. Pillaged tiles only apply pressure (a prosperity penalty that pushes people out). Repairing them removes that pressure, so the city stops bleeding people and recovers prosperity faster, but a repair never adds a population point back. It's a recovery accelerator, not a restore button.
How far can a war shrink a city?

War DISPLACEMENT (people fleeing) is capped at 60% of the city's population when the siege began; the remnant "digs in" and can't be pushed out further. A sustained siege also kills some who can't escape. Those deaths are not bound by the displacement cap or the rural floor, so a long enough siege can wear the city's rural population all the way down, though its urban core and the settlement still stand until an actual capture. The dying builds up gradually rather than all at once, and eases if the siege lifts. Only an actual capture takes the city.
Fastest way to recover a war-torn city?

Relieve the cause so it flips from a net exporter back to a magnet: make peace (violence decays in ~2–3 turns, lifting the war penalty), repair pillaged tiles (removes the lingering pressure), and raise happiness (the biggest prosperity factor: it both stops unhappiness emigration and pulls migrants in).
What happens to a migrant while they're traveling between cities?

Migration isn't instant; it has transit lag. The migrant leaves the source the turn they depart: its rural population point (and that worker's tile yields) is removed right away. They then spend the transit time belonging to NO city, working no tiles, producing nothing, but also costing no upkeep, gold, or happiness. They're added to the destination, which only then gains the yields and pays its one-time integration cost, when they ARRIVE. Transit is 1–4 turns, scaled by distance (~5 hexes per turn, capped at 4); refugees take at least 1 (they camp). Arrival isn't guaranteed: a city can only absorb so many newcomers per turn (the per-city intake cap), so if the destination is full that turn the migrant waits in transit and tries again next turn. And if it was captured or razed while they traveled (or they still can't find room after several turns of waiting) the refugees perish in transit (counted as a loss, not an arrival).
How big is the economic impact of migrants in transit?

Small and self-correcting. Per migrant it's tiny: one rural point's worth of yields suspended for ~1–2 turns (4 at most), and the source was losing that worker anyway, so only the delay before the destination picks them up is truly lost output. In aggregate it's roughly (migrants currently traveling) x (their per-pop yields): a rounding error in peacetime, but a noticeable pool of temporarily-idle population during a big war, since refugees flee every turn and more are in transit at once. It always drains back toward zero within a few turns of migration slowing. This transit lag is also why Emigration can tick up before Immigration catches up: the departure counts now, the arrival lands a few turns later. It does NOT distort Net Migration, which only counts settled cross-civ moves.
Is there a limit on how many people one city gains or loses per turn?

Yes, both ways. A settlement can shed at most a few migration points per turn (so even a besieged city bleeds people steadily instead of emptying in a single catastrophic turn) and it can take in at most a few, so one boomtown can't swallow dozens of newcomers at once. Arrivals over the intake cap simply wait in transit and land on a later turn. Both caps scale with the Emigration intensity preset (Low / Medium / High) and can be fine-tuned individually in Advanced settings. Deaths from war, famine and disaster are a separate channel and aren't counted against either cap.
How does the mod use 1.4.1's happiness, government, and celebration changes?

It reads them directly. Happiness is now a five-stage scale (Angry, Unhappy, Happy, Joyous, Ecstatic) that feeds a city's attractiveness; a civilization in a Celebration (Golden Age) becomes a stronger draw while it lasts; a government's happiness-friendly passives nudge its cities up a little; and empire-wide war weariness adds a push to a war-worn civilization's settlements. 1.4.1 also makes unhappy cities lose more of their yields, which the per-capita prosperity score already picks up.
Did 1.4.1 change how strongly happiness drives migration?

Yes, and the mod was rebalanced for it. Happiness is still the single biggest factor, but it no longer drowns out a city's economy: yields now carry a meaningful share of the decision, so raising a city's production, gold, or food visibly helps it keep and attract people. The rebalance was checked to make sure it doesn't let any civilization snowball, and it can be reverted to the exact pre-1.4.1 behaviour with one Options toggle.
What do the "people" numbers mean, and why are they realistic now?

Civ's population is abstract (1, 2, 3…). The mod turns each point into a representative head-count using Civilization VII's OWN per-era growth math, so the figure reads at a believable historical scale for whatever age you're in: a point leaving a town in Antiquity is a few thousand people, the same point in a sprawling Modern metropolis is far more, and the largest Modern cities reach the real 10–38 million megacity range. It changes smoothly at each age boundary (no sudden jump), two same-size settlements never read identically (the small spread follows their real happiness and urban/rural mix), and the figures match the Demographics mod exactly. Switch between scaled people and the raw Civ numbers any time with the unit toggle.
Does population keep scaling if I play past the end of the game?
Yes. If you keep going on "one more turn" past the natural end, megacities keep growing into a speculative future instead of freezing at the historical cap (bounded so they can't run away).
Can I see refugees a civilization took IN, not just sent out?
Yes. The Graphs tab has both: Refugees Out (people a civilization displaced by war/disaster/conquest) and Refugees In (displaced people it resettled). Each line's tooltip splits the total by cause.
Why did a city suddenly lose a lot of people?

An on-screen toast names the cause (war, disaster, unhappiness, etc.), and the per-city readout breaks down its current pressures. The Notifications tab now keeps the full event ledger, including the narrative Chronicle entries, so you can click any row to see what caused it, where it left, and where the people went.
Can I see which specific war or disaster drove it?

Yes. On the Causes tab, each broad cause (War, Disaster, Unhappiness…) drills down to the SPECIFIC events behind it (a named war, a particular eruption/flood, or the active age crisis), with each event's emigration and deaths. An age crisis is attributed to itself: an Invasion crisis shows under War, a Plague crisis under Disaster, a Loyalty/Revolt crisis under Unhappiness, so you can see exactly how much of a civilization's movement a single crisis caused. A war refugee event names both sides when you've met them, and reads "<Civ> vs. an unmet civilization" when you have not, so a war is always named without revealing a civilization you haven't met.
What is the Ethnic Composition lens showing?

Each settlement painted by where its people came from. Rather than one flat colour per city, every owned tile is shaded by an origin and by how densely it's populated: the urban core reads vivid in the dominant origin's colour, worked rural tiles fainter, and smaller communities are spread across the city. Diaspora tiles stay clearly coloured rather than fading out, so even a small immigrant community reads on the map, while a genuinely single-origin city still correctly shows one colour. Each origin's share of the population is preserved across the tiles, and a city founded by one civilization, half-emptied by war, then captured and regrown shows the captor's colour strengthening over time, the demographic shift, on the map. Press Shift+E to toggle it.

A written history of the world's great migrations, recorded as it happens. As large waves move, it captures the moments worth keeping, a city emptied by war or disaster, a diaspora taking root far from home, a people returning once their homeland recovered, each as a short line of prose. Each line is drawn from the settlement's real surroundings (a diaspora settling "by the harbour" or "beyond the granaries" only when that city actually has a coast or a granary) so the prose never invents a feature the place doesn't have, and it reads at the city's edge, exactly where the lens paints the newcomers. These appear in the Notifications tab as "Chronicle" entries, alongside the per-event detail, so the whole story lives in one place.
A pop-up asked me what to do about refugees, what is that?

A refugee decision. When a real upheaval (a neighbour taking several cities in a short span, or a plague crisis) sends a wave toward your lands, you're occasionally asked how to receive them: welcome them in (a small gold cost, and they settle among you and, in time, become your people), settle them on the frontier, or turn them away. The effects are light and the event is rare, a few times an age at most. Turn the whole thing off under Options ▸ Mods ▸ Emigration ▸ refugee decisions.

All three are on by default and each has its own switch under Options ▸ Mods ▸ Emigration: "ethnic integration" (newcomers drifting toward the host identity), "return migration" (diasporas going home), and "refugee decisions" (the occasional pop-up). The Ethnic Composition lens is always available, and Chronicle entries are recorded in the Notifications tab.

When a foreign community grows large enough to become a lasting, established part of one of your cities — a real standing presence, not just a lot of past arrivals — it takes root as a Cultural Enclave on a district at the city's edge, named for the origin people (the Roman Enclave, the Punic Enclave, and so on). You're offered a one-time choice of how the city makes room for it. It's on by default; turn it off under Options ▸ Mods ▸ Emigration ▸ cultural enclaves.

There's no strictly best option. Your chosen stance then applies its small yields every turn, so the enclave actually reads in the city, not just once. Dismiss the modal (Escape or click outside) and it settles into the quiet "let them be."
What's the quote below the prose?

A single real, attributed historical quote for the enclave, shown as a page of history — in the origin people's own language followed by an English translation (Greek, Chinese, Persian, Latin, Old Norse, and many more), each verified against a primary source. An origin has two quotes: its first enclave shows one, its second shows the other.
How many enclaves can one civilization have?

At most two in your whole empire — but that's PER civilization, not overall. You can hold two Roman and two Norman and two Han enclaves at the same time; reaching the cap for one origin never blocks a different one. A different people overtaking an existing enclave's tile is a change of hands (the Chronicle notes it and you choose again), not a third stacked enclave.
What happens if I go to war with an enclave's homeland?

The enclave turns "contested": its yield benefit is reduced and a small, capped happiness strain applies while the war lasts, framed as the city's wartime unease falling on families who did not choose the fighting — not as the enclave being disloyal. It contributes fully again once peace returns.
